# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`

`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`

`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Current state:
- `model_request_summary` carries the per-message summaries (bounded by gh-1073 cap: 64 messages / 256 KiB budget) — this is still WAY too big for marathon sessions (1101 requests × 256 KiB = ~280 MB). The wire dump records (2 MB cap each) are also written inline when `wireDump` is on. Prompt/manifest blobs are deduped but can each be huge (uncapped system prompt, full tool manifests with 2 KiB schemas per tool — with 20+ tools, 100+ KB per version, many versions).
- Usage data (tokens, latency, model, finish reason) — where does that live? Let me check: usage fold reads `model_request_summary` records. Let me look at what fields the usage scanner reads from model_request_summary.

So the plan per the ticket:

**Part 1 — lightweight `model_request_summary` in the primary JSONL.**
- Strip the heavy per-message `messages` (block texts) from the record; keep counts/sizes/hashes + usage metadata (tokens, latency, model ID, finish reason).

**Part 2 — blob directory `.fah/trajectories/<sid>/requests/`** with TTL/rotation.

Design: introduce a `TrajectoryRequestBlobStore` (IO) that:
- Writes heavy payloads (per-message block texts + wire dumps + maybe prompt/manifest blobs) to `<blobRoot>/<sessionId>/requests/<seq>-<hash>.json`.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two

|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value

`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

description: >

  persists (themes also via ~/.fah/themes/*.json), never by guessing keys.
argument-hint: "[what to configure, e.g. 'point project memory at ./memory']"

  - config
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`

array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`

`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Let me define the actual change:

### Design

**Goal**: primary session JSONL stops carrying heavy per-request raw payload dumps; they move to a per-session blob directory with TTL/rotation.

**1. `TrajectoryRequestDetail` gains a spilt form (gh-1745):**

The heavy part of a `model_request_summary` record is `messages[].blocks[].text` (+ previews). The ticket wants lightweight metadata only: counts, sizes, hashes, plus a pointer to where the full detail lives. Add to `TrajectoryRequestDetail`:
- `messagesBlobFile` (String?) — file NAME within the session's trajectory requests dir holding the full per-message summaries.
- `inputChars` total? The usage scanner sums `messages[].chars` — I'll add a top-level `messagesChars` int so the stub keeps the estimate basis without any messages array. Wait, but the stub messages list is still needed for... the Request tab renders per-message rows. On replay from the JSONL only, with spill, we lose per-message rows unless hydrated. Hmm.

Wait — how important is it to keep the Request tab fully functional on replay? There's a tension:
- Keep full `messages` in JSONL → bloat (the ticket).
- Move to blob dir → JSONL is lightweight; Request tab needs the blob to render fully.

For hydration: the snapshot builder is PURE (no IO). The CLI `/trajectory` and the app build snapshots from session records. Hydrating spilled request details would need an async IO pass after the snapshot build. That's a bigger refactor of every consumer.

Pragmatic middle ground (and what I think the ticket actually wants — the numbers are about marathon sessions):

- **The heavy payloads (per-message block texts and wire dumps) go to the blob dir.** The in-JSONL `model_request_summary` keeps: counts, sizes (messageCount, systemPromptChars, toolCount, toolNames, per-message role+chars+preview... hmm preview is 200 chars per message — with 100 messages that's 200 KB per record again!).

Hmm wait. Let me recompute what's big in a record:
- Per message: role + chars + preview (≤200) + blocks (each ≤8192 text + ~100 overhead).
- gh-1073 caps full messages at 64 / 256 KiB; older degrade to role+chars+preview='' — tiny stubs.
- So after gh-1073, a record is ≤ ~256 KiB, typically much smaller... except the cap walks `weight = preview + sum(block.text)` — capped at 256 KiB per record. 1101 records × 256 KiB = 287 MB worst case. Typical marathon: blocks get hit (8 KiB tool results are common in coding sessions) → each record realistically ~100-250 KB → 1101 × ~200 KB ≈ 220 MB. Plus wire dumps (2 MB each) → hundreds of MB more. So the ticket's 658 MB figure is plausibly post-gh-1073 too (or pre; doesn't matter).

The fix must make the JSONL record O(1KB): role/chars stubs and metadata only, with full block texts spilled.

**Decision on the messages array in JSONL**: keep messages as TINY stubs (role + chars only, no preview, no blocks) when spilling, and put the FULL detail (previews + blocks) into the blob file. This keeps:

Spilling to disk with rotation budget 50 MB — a cap on the blob payload keeps things sane. Actually the cap exists precisely to bound the payload; apply it to the spilled detail too (newest 64 messages full). Hmm, but that loses old messages' previews in the blob. The cap's stub degradation (role+chars, preview:') is what today's JSONL gets. For the blob, I'd rather keep the FULL uncapped detail? No — keep the cap; it's the established bound and the Request tab only ever showed the capped view. Consistency: the blob carries exactly what today's JSONL record would have carried (capped detail); the JSONL record carries the stub-only version. Zero behavior change for renders that get the blob hydrated; a lighter degradation for ones that don't.

Wait, actually — simpler and better: keep `capTrajectoryRequestDetail` applied as today (in `_captureRequest`). The blob file then contains the capped detail JSON (what would have been persisted inline). The JSONL record contains the same detail minus the heavy text: per message keep role+chars (drop preview+blocks), plus `blob` pointer `{file, chars}`.

  persists (themes also via ~/.fah/themes/*.json), never by guessing keys.

user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).
