# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the

Now I have a full picture. Time to decide the implementation scope. This is a big-ticket performance item; the deliverable per the general guidelines: implement with TDD in `test/`, follow existing patterns, all tests pass, PR description in outputs/response.md.

Let me define the actual change:

### Design

**Goal**: primary session JSONL stops carrying heavy per-request raw payload dumps; they move to a per-session blob directory with TTL/rotation.

**1. `TrajectoryRequestDetail` gains a spilt form (gh-1745):**

The heavy part of a `model_request_summary` record is `messages[].blocks[].text` (+ previews). The ticket wants lightweight metadata only: counts, sizes, hashes, plus a pointer to where the full detail lives. Add to `TrajectoryRequestDetail`:
- `messagesBlobFile` (String?) — file NAME within the session's trajectory requests dir holding the full per-message summaries.
- `inputChars` total? The usage scanner sums `messages[].chars` — I'll add a top-level `messagesChars` int so the stub keeps the estimate basis without any messages array. Wait, but the stub messages list is still needed for... the Request tab renders per-message rows. On replay from the JSONL only, with spill, we lose per-message rows unless hydrated. Hmm.

Wait — how important is it to keep the Request tab fully functional on replay? There's a tension:
- Keep full `messages` in JSONL → bloat (the ticket).
- Move to blob dir → JSONL is lightweight; Request tab needs the blob to render fully.

For hydration: the snapshot builder is PURE (no IO). The CLI `/trajectory` and the app build snapshots from session records. Hydrating spilled request details would need an async IO pass after the snapshot build. That's a bigger refactor of every consumer.

Pragmatic middle ground (and what I think the ticket actually wants — the numbers are about marathon sessions):

- **The heavy payloads (per-message block texts and wire dumps) go to the blob dir.** The in-JSONL `model_request_summary` keeps: counts, sizes (messageCount, systemPromptChars, toolCount, toolNames, per-message role+chars+preview... hmm preview is 200 chars per message — with 100 messages that's 200 KB per record again!).

Hmm wait. Let me recompute what's big in a record:
- Per message: role + chars + preview (≤200) + blocks (each ≤8192 text + ~100 overhead).
- gh-1073 caps full messages at 64 / 256 KiB; older degrade to role+chars+preview='' — tiny stubs.
- So after gh-1073, a record is ≤ ~256 KiB, typically much smaller... except the cap walks `weight = preview + sum(block.text)` — capped at 256 KiB per record. 1101 records × 256 KiB = 287 MB worst case. Typical marathon: blocks get hit (8 KiB tool results are common in coding sessions) → each record realistically ~100-250 KB → 1101 × ~200 KB ≈ 220 MB. Plus wire dumps (2 MB each) → hundreds of MB more. So the ticket's 658 MB figure is plausibly post-gh-1073 too (or pre; doesn't matter).

The fix must make the JSONL record O(1KB): role/chars stubs and metadata only, with full block texts spilled.

**Decision on the messages array in JSONL**: keep messages as TINY stubs (role + chars only, no preview, no blocks) when spilling, and put the FULL detail (previews + blocks) into the blob file. This keeps:
- The Request tab on replay: shows per-message size rows (sizes truthful) — the "details" texts require the blob. The trajectory fold uses `requestDetail` for the Request tab; renders must tolerate missing block texts (they already do — old sessions (E6) render exactly as today with empty blocks).
- The usage scanner's `inputChars` estimate: still works via `messages[].chars` sums.
- The gh-1073 cap (`capTrajectoryRequestDetail`) stays as a backstop for the BLOB write (bounding what goes to disk) — hmm, actually the cap should still apply to the blob content: a 100-message request's full detail would be ~1-9 MB (gh-1073 mentions 0.5 MB per record for 1030 messages). Spilling to disk with rotation budget 50 MB — a cap on the blob payload keeps things sane. Actually the cap exists precisely to bound the payload; apply it to the spilled detail too (newest 64 messages full). Hmm, but that loses old messages' previews in the blob. The cap's stub degradation (role+chars, preview:') is what today's JSONL gets. For the blob, I'd rather keep the FULL uncapped detail? No — keep the cap; it's the established bound and the Request tab only ever showed the capped view. Consistency: the blob carries exactly what today's JSONL record would have carried (capped detail); the JSONL record carries the stub-only version. Zero behavior change for renders that get the blob hydrated; a lighter degradation for ones that don't.

Wait, actually — simpler and better: keep `capTrajectoryRequestDetail` applied as today (in `_captureRequest`). The blob file then contains the capped detail JSON (what would have been persisted inline). The JSONL record contains the same detail minus the heavy text: per message keep role+chars (drop preview+blocks), plus `blob` pointer `{file, chars}`.

Hmm, but previews (≤200 chars × 64 messages ≈ 13 KB) — "lightweight metadata" per the ticket is tokens/latency/model/finish reason. The previews are part of the "raw prompt dumps" family. I'll spill previews too (they're in the blob's full detail), keeping the JSONL record to pure sizes/counts/pointers. That matches "Store only lightweight metadata".

**2. Wire dumps** (`trajectory_wire_dump` records, 2 MB cap each): also spill to the blob dir. The in-JSONL record — should it exist at all? The summary already points at the dump via `wireDumpHash`. If dumps move to files, the JSONL `trajectory_wire_dump` record becomes a tiny pointer record OR we skip it and reference the file. The blob TABLE in the snapshot (`TrajectoryBlobTable.wireDumps`) is used by renders (Request tab "raw" view). If the dump is on disk, the table can't have the payload...

This is getting big. Let me scope precisely:

**Scope decision**: Introduce `TrajectoryRequestBlobStore` (gh-1745) in `lib/src/trajectory/trajectory_request_blobs.dart`:

Configurable via config section `trajectory:` — hmm, need to check existing config naming. Let me look for an existing trajectory config section... There's `wireDump` flag in AgentLoopConfig. Let me check where config parsing for trajectory lives.
 - Reads: `read(file)` → the full detail for hydration.

- The persister (`TrajectoryBlobPersister.recordsFor`) — hmm, but the persister is PURE (no IO; the doc says "Pure data + pure functions: no IO"). The hosts do the IO. So the spill store is a HOST-side helper: hosts call `store.persistRequest(...)` which (a) writes the blob file, (b) returns the records to append (with the light summary + pointer), or a degraded inline fallback when the write fails.

Where does the store get its root? `.fah/trajectories/<sid>/requests/` — relative to the project root (ExecutionEnv cwd), same convention as spills (`.fah/spills/<sessionId>/`). Let me check the spill store for the root resolution pattern.

But prompts grow with project context and manifests change with tools; a long session can mint many versions (each AGENTS.md edit, MCP connect, etc.). Each version can be 100 KB+. The ticket doesn't name them explicitly ("raw prompt/completion dumps"). Moving them to disk too... name: self-settings
description: >
  Configure fa (flutter_agent_harness) itself by editing the exact config
  files the CLI settings commands write: provider/model selection and roles,
  memory paths, tool availability, cubes, MCP servers, redaction, skills
  access, approval and mode, themes and TUI appearance (tui.theme: switch
  or create a theme). Use when asked to reconfigure fa without a human
  in the REPL ("switch us to provider X", "point project memory at this
  path", "disable web_search for this project", "switch the theme to
  ohmypi").
when_to_use: Reconfiguring fa itself — settings, provider, models, memory,
  tools, cubes, MCP, redaction, skills access, themes/TUI appearance — on
  any host (CLI headless, REPL, app), by editing the YAML config the CLI
  persists (themes also via ~/.fah/themes/*.json), never by guessing keys.
argument-hint: "[what to configure, e.g. 'point project memory at ./memory']"
allowed-tools:
  - read
  - write
  - edit
  - ls
  - bash
  - config
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two

3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before

   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Implementation plan (gh-1745)

### Part A — `TrajectoryRequestDetail` spilt form

Add to `TrajectoryRequestDetail`:
- `spillFile` (String?) — path of the blob file in `.fah/trajectories/<sid>/requests/` holding the FULL detail (+ optional wire dump).
- Add `fromJson`/`toJson` support.

Add a pure function `stripTrajectoryRequestDetail(detail, {spillFile})` → detail with per-message `preview: ''` and `blocks: []` (role+chars stubs only). Keep counts/sizes/hashes — usage estimation (`messages[].chars`) and the ledger's Request-tab size table still work.

Also the ticket's lightweight metadata: "tokens, latency, model ID, finish reason". Do we have those at request-capture time? No — they're known after the response. Where do they live today? In the assistant message record: `usage`, `model`, and the trajectory fold computes latency from timestamps? Let me check what `TrajectoryAssistantRecord` has — `stepStartTime`, `firstTokenTime`, `completedTime`... wait those were in the record class. Let me check how the app/CLI persist those timestamps. Actually those timestamps are `DateTime?` fields on `TrajectoryToolRecord` (for tools). For assistant requests, `TrajectoryRequestFacts`... let me not go down this hole — the summary record already sits before the assistant message which carries usage/model/finishReason. The usage fold already reads tokens from the assistant message. Adding tokens/latency/finish-reason to the summary would duplicate data already in the JSONL (assistant `message` record has `usage`, `model`; `stopReason`?).

Hmm, let me check if the assistant message record carries finishReason. If the ticket's "lightweight metadata" list is the shape of the NEW record, I should make sure those specific fields exist. Let me check `AssistantMessage`: `model`, `provider`, `usage`, `responseId`... `stopReason`? Let me grep.

Good — the assistant message record already carries tokens (`usage`), model ID (`model`/`responseModel`), and finish reason (`stopReason`/`rawStopReason`) in the primary JSONL, paired with the request summary. The "lightweight metadata" in the ticket is thus: counts/sizes/hashes + the spill pointer; tokens/latency/model/finishReason stay available from the adjacent assistant record. The test rig pattern is clear. Now I have everything needed to write the plan and implement. Let me set up my working plan:

## Implementation plan (gh-1745)

### New file: `lib/src/trajectory/trajectory_request_blobs.dart`
Pure-core + ExecutionEnv IO (like spill.dart):
1. `trajectorySpillDir(sessionId)` → `.fah/trajectories/<sid>/requests` (sessionless fallback).
2. `stripTrajectoryRequestDetail(detail, {required String spillFile})` → stub-messages copy with `spillFile` set. (Maybe in trajectory_record.dart next to cap — better there; it mutates the same class.)
3. `TrajectoryRequestDetail.spillFile` + `spillChars`? Let me add just `spillFile`. Also `wireDumpHash` exists already.
4. `TrajectoryRequestSpillResult` — `file` + `wireDumpHash` (empty when no dump).
5. `TrajectoryRequestBlobStore`:
  - ctor: `env`, `sessionId` lazy, `maxBytes` (default `trajectoryBlobMaxBytes = 50 << 20`), `ttl` (default `trajectoryBlobTtl = Duration(days: 30)`), `clock`.
  - `Future<TrajectoryRequestSpillResult?> write({required TrajectoryRequestDetail detail, String? rawWireDump, String Function(String)? redact})`.
    - serialize `{detail: detail.toJson(), if wireDump: 'wireDump': dump.toJson()}`; pretty or compact? compact (bytes). Write `<dir>/<seq>.json`.
    - seq: lazily initialize from one listDir (max numeric stem + 1), then increment; reset on session change.
    - on write failure → null (caller falls back to legacy inline).
    - after success → `enforceBudget(dir)` (bounded: only when `_bytesSinceEnforce > maxBytes` OR first write; plus TTL sweep on each enforce).
  - `Future<TrajectoryRequestDetail?> readDetail(String path)`, `Future<TrajectoryWireDump?> readWireDump(String path)`.
  - `enforceBudget`: listDir; parse mtime/size; delete files older than ttl (relative to clock()); then delete oldest until total ≤ maxBytes. Return count.
6. Kill-switch note in docs.

### `trajectory_record.dart`
- `TrajectoryRequestDetail`: add `spillFile` (String?), toJson/fromJson.

/// Defaults
const int trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes = 50 << 20; // 50 MB

class TrajectoryRequestSpill {

}

class TrajectoryRequestBlobStore {

   required ExecutionEnv env,
   required String? Function() sessionId,
   int maxBytes = trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes,
   int ttlDays = trajectoryRequestBlobTtlDays,
   DateTime Function()? clock,
 });

 });

 Future<int> enforceBudget(); // sweep ttl + size, returns deleted count
}
``

write() logic:
- sid = sessionId(); if sid changed since last → reset counter AND re-init (counter probe per dir anyway).
- seq: lazily probe the dir once per session (listDir, max numeric stem + 1). If listDir fails (missing dir) → start at 1.

- payload: jsonEncode({'detail': detail.toJson(), if (dump != null) 'wireDump': dump.toJson()}).
- path = `.fah/trajectories/<sid|sessionless>/requests/<seq>.json`; writeBinaryFile; Err → return null.
- track `_bytesSinceSweep += payload.length`; if `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` → enforceBudget() (and reset the tracker). Hmm — enforce at each write is O(files); throttle to when the tracker crosses maxBytes. But TTL expiry then only happens on crossing — a slow session never sweeps. TTL sweep on a TIME trigger: sweep when `now - _lastSweep > 1h` (clock seam) OR bytes crossed. Good.
- return TrajectoryRequestSpill(file: path, wireDumpHash: dump?.hash).

enforceBudget():
- listDir(dir); entries with numeric `.json` names; total size; delete (remove force) files older than ttlDays (clock() - mtime > ttl) first; then while total > maxBytes delete oldest-by-mtime. Return deleted count.

- return TrajectoryRequestSpill(file: path, wireDumpHash: dump?.hash).

- listDir(dir); entries with numeric `.json` names; total size; delete (remove force) files older than ttlDays (clock() - mtime > ttl) first; then while total > maxBytes delete oldest-by-mtime. Return deleted count.

```dart
/// Defaults
const int trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes = 50 << 20; // 50 MB
const int trajectoryRequestBlobTtlDays = 30;
const String trajectoryRequestsBlobDirRoot = '.fah/trajectories';

String trajectoryRequestBlobDir(String? sessionId) =>
 '$trajectoryRequestBlobDirRoot/${sessionId ?? 'sessionless'}/requests';

class TrajectoryRequestSpill {
 final String file; // relative path written
 final String? wireDumpHash; // hash of the dumped wire payload, null when none
}

class TrajectoryRequestBlobStore {
 TrajectoryRequestBlobStore({
   required ExecutionEnv env,
   required String? Function() sessionId,
   int maxBytes = trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes,
   int ttlDays = trajectoryRequestBlobTtlDays,
   DateTime Function()? clock,
 });

 Future<TrajectoryRequestSpill?> write({
   required TrajectoryRequestDetail detail,
   String? rawWireDump,
   String Function(String)? redactWireDump,
 });

 Future<TrajectoryRequestDetail?> readDetail(String path);
 Future<TrajectoryWireDump?> readWireDump(String path);
 Future<int> enforceBudget(); // sweep ttl + size, returns deleted count
}
``

write() logic:
- sid = sessionId(); if sid changed since last → reset counter AND re-init (counter probe per dir anyway).
- seq: lazily probe the dir once per session (listDir, max numeric stem + 1). If listDir fails (missing dir) → start at 1.
- build dump: `rawWireDump == null ? null : trajectoryBuildWireDump(rawWireDump, redact: redactWireDump)`.
- payload: jsonEncode({'detail': detail.toJson(), if (dump != null) 'wireDump': dump.toJson()}).
- path = `.fah/trajectories/<sid|sessionless>/requests/<seq>.json`; writeBinaryFile; Err → return null.
- track `_bytesSinceSweep += payload.length`; if `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` → enforceBudget() (and reset the tracker). Hmm — enforce at each write is O(files); throttle to when the tracker crosses maxBytes. But TTL expiry then only happens on crossing — a slow session never sweeps. TTL sweep on a TIME trigger: sweep when `now - _lastSweep > 1h` (clock seam) OR bytes crossed. Good.
- return TrajectoryRequestSpill(file: path, wireDumpHash: dump?.hash).

enforceBudget():
- listDir(dir); entries with numeric `.json` names; total size; delete (remove force) files older than ttlDays (clock() - mtime > ttl) first; then while total > maxBytes delete oldest-by-mtime. Return deleted count.

/// Defaults
const int trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes = 50 << 20; // 50 MB
const int trajectoryRequestBlobTtlDays = 30;
const String trajectoryRequestsBlobDirRoot = '.fah/trajectories';

String trajectoryRequestBlobDir(String? sessionId) =>
 '$trajectoryRequestBlobDirRoot/${sessionId ?? 'sessionless'}/requests';

class TrajectoryRequestSpill {
 final String file; // relative path written
 final String? wireDumpHash; // hash of the dumped wire payload, null when none
}

class TrajectoryRequestBlobStore {
 TrajectoryRequestBlobStore({
   required ExecutionEnv env,
   required String? Function() sessionId,
   int maxBytes = trajectoryRequestBlobMaxBytes,
   int ttlDays = trajectoryRequestBlobTtlDays,
   DateTime Function()? clock,
 });

 Future<TrajectoryRequestSpill?> write({
   required TrajectoryRequestDetail detail,
   String? rawWireDump,
   String Function(String)? redactWireDump,
 });

 Future<TrajectoryRequestDetail?> readDetail(String path);
 Future<TrajectoryWireDump?> readWireDump(String path);
 Future<int> enforceBudget(); // sweep ttl + size, returns deleted count
}
``

write() logic:
- sid = sessionId(); if sid changed since last → reset counter AND re-init (counter probe per dir anyway).
- seq: lazily probe the dir once per session (listDir, max numeric stem + 1). If listDir fails (missing dir) → start at 1.
- build dump: `rawWireDump == null ? null : trajectoryBuildWireDump(rawWireDump, redact: redactWireDump)`.
- payload: jsonEncode({'detail': detail.toJson(), if (dump != null) 'wireDump': dump.toJson()}).
- path = `.fah/trajectories/<sid|sessionless>/requests/<seq>.json`; writeBinaryFile; Err → return null.
- track `_bytesSinceSweep += payload.length`; if `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` → enforceBudget() (and reset the tracker). Hmm — enforce at each write is O(files); throttle to when the tracker crosses maxBytes. But TTL expiry then only happens on crossing — a slow session never sweeps. TTL sweep on a TIME trigger: sweep when `now - _lastSweep > 1h` (clock seam) OR bytes crossed. Good.
- return TrajectoryRequestSpill(file: path, wireDumpHash: dump?.hash).

enforceBudget():
- listDir(dir); entries with numeric `.json` names; total size; delete (remove force) files older than ttlDays (clock() - mtime > ttl) first; then while total > maxBytes delete oldest-by-mtime. Return deleted count.

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

messages.preview: Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:

blocks.text:
Two failures:

1. **Rotation test**: expected `['3.json']`, got `[]` — all three deleted. Why? My sweep triggers when `_bytesSinceSweep >= maxBytes` — with maxBytes=1 every write sweeps; the sweep deletes files while `total > maxBytes`. After writing 3.json, total is (1.json + 2.json + 3.json) > 1 → oldest-first delete: 1, 2, then 3?? total after deleting 1 and 2 is still > 1 (3.json's size), so 3 gets deleted too. The budget semantics: "keep last N MB" — the newest file must survive even if alone it exceeds the budget. Fix: never delete the NEWEST file (skip it in the sweep). Standard rotation: delete oldest files until total fits OR only the newest remains.

2. **TL test**: `1.json` should be expired (written at t0 with clock t0; clock moved to t0+31d; write 2 happens at t0+31d — 1.json age = 31d > 30d TTL → delete). Got both files. Why didn't the sweep run? `_maybeSweep`: `_bytesSinceSweep < maxBytes && !hourElapsed` → hourElapsed is true (31 days), so sweep SHOULD run... unless `_lastSweepAt` was set on write 1 — no: after write 1, `_maybeSweep` runs (hourElapsed: last==null → true) → sweep at t0 (nothing to delete — 1.json age 0) → `_lastSweepAt = t0`. At write 2: hourElapsed = 31d ≥ 1h → sweep runs. enforceBudget: ttl 30d, 1.json mtime = t0, now = t0+31d → expired → remove. So why did it stay?

Hmm — MemoryExecutionEnv mtime: does writeFile set mtime = wall clock NOW or the test clock? The store's clock seam returns my fake `current`, but MemoryExecutionEnv's file mtime uses the REAL clock (DateTime.now). Real now is 2026-ish; my test clock says 2026-01-01 → 1.json's real mtime is "now" (2026-xx actual date, later than 2026-01-01?) → age = now(clock) - mtime(real) = negative → not expired. I need `env.setMtime(path, ms)` (test-only helper, saw it at memory_execution_env.dart:236). Fix the test: after write 1, setMtime 1.json to the fake t0; keep clock consistent.

Also fix 1 (newest survives). Update enforceBudget: skip index 0 (newest = last in oldest-first sorted? no — sorted oldest-first, newest is LAST). Delete only from the front, and stop before deleting the last remaining file: `for (var i = 0; i < sorted.length - 1; i++)`. Even when ALL are expired, keep the newest (the blob the just-written summary points at... actually the newest at sweep time might not be the one just written if sweep runs later; but keeping the newest is the "keep last N" semantic — good).

Wait — the TTL test expects `['2.json']` — 1.json expired → deleted; 2.json (newest) kept. With "never delete newest": loop `i < sorted.length - 1` → 1.json deleted (expired), stop. Good.

Rotation test: writes 1,2,3 each ~2-3KB. After write 3: sweep; sorted=[1,2,3]; loop i<2: 1.json deleted (total>max), 2.json deleted (total>max — total now = size(3) > 1) → stop at i=1 (can't delete newest 3). Result ['3.json'].

Edge: what if expired files include the newest? Newest survives — acceptable (it's the live head; the next sweep after it ages will remove it).
Two issues: the sweep must never delete the newest blob, and the TTL test needs `setMtime` (memory fs uses the real clock). Fixing both:
